title: Hiskalelus of the sefiros: bittul in the opposite, light in a vessel, and the essence turned by mesirus nefesh
overview:
Now comes what we have all been waiting for: how the ten *sefiros* of *Atzilus* are included in one another, down to *chesed* of *Malchus* of *chachma*. Each *sefira* divides into ten and ten into ten, the *sefira* and the *partzuf*; in the *etzem hamidda* itself a bias turns every point to its own side, like a bribed judge, and only as it spreads out can it compromise.

The first kind of *hiskalelus* is *bittul*: the prosecutor becomes the defender, sugar overpowers cocoa, the murderer's childhood becomes the reason to throw the book at him. It works because each side hides its opposite. The second kind is a light in a vessel, where the opposite strengthens: feeding your hungry enemy, the spy, the raise before the firing, the father who rebukes because he loves, the harsh cure. Like red ink spelling "green", light and vessel do not contradict, so both can come at once. In the simple points nothing combines, except through *mesirus nefesh*, which makes even sins into merits. From it come three ways of *avoda*: trust past the vessel, a light that overpowers, and enjoying the challenge itself.

terms.gloss: inclusion: one attribute included in another, from a nullification in it to working together with it
division: each sefira divided into ten, and each of those into ten again
the essence of the attribute: a bias that turns every point to its own side and has no recognizable division
nullification: here a thing totally turned over into its opposite, which it can be only because the opposite is hidden in it
gevura of chesed: as light in a vessel, kindness done in the garment of judgment, the strongest kindness
chesed of gevura: as light in a vessel, judgment done by way of kindness, the strongest judgment
matter and form: like ink and the word it spells, a light and its vessel do not contradict
a kind finds its kind and wakes up: a nullified thing returns when it meets its own kind
self-sacrifice: the soul's connection to G-d Himself, above the division of chesed and gevura
a returnee to Judaism, in whom even the essence of bad is turned to good

sections.title: Every sefira divides into ten and ten into ten, but in the essence a bias turns everything to its side
sections.summary: Before the kinds of *hiskalelus* (inclusion) can be explained, each *sefira* has to be divided into ten and each of those into ten again, the *sefira* and the *partzuf*. In the *etzem hamidda* (the essence of the attribute) there is no recognizable division, and like a bribe it turns every point to its own side; only once it spreads out can it compromise.

phrases.en: Now that we've explained everything

phrases.he: יש להבין בפרטי התכללות דעשר ספירות דאצילות
phrases.en: We have to understand the particular types of interclusion, interrelationship, or *hiskalelus* between the ten *sefiros* of *Atzilus*.

blocks.text:
**Now that we've explained everything**: from the *Atzmus Ein Sof*, the *reshimu* (the impression left after the *tzimtzum*), the *Kav*, the *roshem* before it; how *Adam Kadmon* lights up *Atzilus* in a way of *gilui ha'helem* (revelation of what is hidden); the *Akudim*, *Nekudim* and *Berudim*, *nekuda*, *sefira* and *partzuf*; and how from the outer side of the *Keser* it splits up into three lines.

Now comes what we have all been waiting for. **We have to understand the particular types of interclusion, interrelationship, or hiskalelus between the ten sefiros of Atzilus.** That means that now we are going to explain what *chesed* of *gevura* and *gevura* of *chesed* mean, all the way until we will be able to understand what it means *chesed* of *Malchus* of *chachma* of *Malchus* of *chesed*, as was said at the beginning of chapter 10.

phrases.en: but first

phrases.he: יש לבאר ענין פרטי התחלקות הספירות לי' וי' לי' כו'
phrases.en: First we have to understand how each *sefira* divides into ten, and each of those ten divides into ten further.

phrases.he: כמו חסד שבחכמה שנחלק גם הוא לי', וכהאי גוונא גבורה שבחכמה נחלק לי' כו'.

blocks.text: **But first**, before the kinds of inclusion, **we have to understand how each sefira divides into ten, and each of those ten divides into ten further.** For example, *chachma* (wisdom) has ten *sefiros*: *Keser* of *chachma*, *chachma* of *chachma*, *bina* of *chachma*, *daas* of *chachma*, *chesed* of *chachma*, *gevura* of *chachma*. After you have divided *chachma* into ten, you can take each of those ten and divide it into ten. Within *chesed* of *chachma* itself there is *Keser* of *chesed* of *chachma*, *chachma* of *chesed* of *chachma*, all ten; and the same with *gevura* of *chachma*. And really you can divide each of those into tens of tens and go forever, infinitely. But usually we only divide it twice. We usually only go to a hundred.

The reason we usually go to a hundred is what this chapter will explain: there are two main types of *hiskalelus*. We count one division for the first type and the other division for the second type.

By the way, this connects back to what was explained in chapter 20 about *nekuda*, *sefira*, *partzuf*. When we just count the *sefira*, *chachma*, that is like one *nekuda* (a point). When we divide it into ten in the first way, that is what we call a *sefira*. And when we divide it into ten again in the next way, that is called a *partzuf*. That is usually the way it works in *Kabbala*. So first comes a general explanation of the division of ten into ten, and then the two main types of *hiskalelus*.

phrases.en: because *chachma* includes ten *sefiros*, ten subdivisions.

blocks.text: **Because chachma includes ten sefiros**, ten subdivisions. **For example, there's chesed and gevura of chachma.** What does *chesed* and *gevura* of *chachma* mean? To lean towards *zechus* (merit) or towards *chov* (guilt). You can have a *chachma*, **an intuitive intellect that leans towards merit or towards guilt.**

blocks.title: My better judgment tells me
blocks.text: Somebody asks you, "Do you think this is a good idea?" Even if you cannot explain it in *bina*, you do not know why you think it is good or bad, you have a feeling. You say, "Well, you know, my better judgment tells me it's not really a good idea. It doesn't give me a good feeling." Or sometimes you say, "Yeah, that just seems right. I have a feeling that that's the right thing to do." Or a judge: sometimes he cannot explain why, but he feels that this person is innocent, or that this person is guilty. Those are *chesed* and *gevura* of *chachma*.

phrases.en: Let's say we're talking of *chesed d'chachma*: the person thinks that he's innocent, he thinks that it's a good thing.
That itself also has ten.
for example, there's *chesed* and *gevura* of *chesed d'chachma*.

phrases.he: לזכות באופן כך וכך, ולחוב יחייב גם הוא באופן כך וכך

blocks.text: Take *chesed d'chachma*: the person thinks the man is innocent, that it is a good thing. **That itself also has ten**: **there's chesed and gevura of chesed d'chachma.** You are going to say he won the court case, but there are different ways of *zechus*. You can say, "Okay, he's not really guilty, so we're letting him off, but he's not a hero either." That is *gevura* of *chesed d'chachma*. Or you can say, "No, not only should he not be punished, and not only is he innocent, he should be rewarded." That is *chesed* of *chesed d'chachma*.

phrases.en: even though you're going to say, well, wait a minute, but in *gevura* of *chachma*, whatever you're going to say is a merit, *gevura* of *chachma* is going to look at as a bad, negative point.
and any type of *chov* you're going to say is going to be turned into a merit by *chesed d'chachma*.

blocks.text: The parenthesis raises an objection. **Even though you're going to say, well, wait a minute**: **in gevura of chachma, whatever you're going to say is a merit, gevura of chachma is going to look at as a bad, negative point.** The same point that is brought up can be looked at both ways.

blocks.title: The murderer's childhood
blocks.text:
Somebody was convicted of, let's say, a murder, and in his defense they say: "You have to appreciate where he's coming from. He was brought up in a very bad environment, his whole life he had these bad influences, his parents traumatized him. What do you expect? Somebody brought up like that, it's not really his fault; he was driven to be like this. He was already depressed and angry." That is brought up as a merit, and it comes from *chesed d'chachma*.

But *gevura* of *chachma* is going to say: "Yeah, that's right. That shows you that he's rotten to the core! Not only did he make a bad choice; from the day he was born he was deteriorated from all sides, his whole moral framework was perverted, there's no hope for him at all, there's nothing positive left in him for society. We should definitely throw the book at him." So the same point is looked at both as a *zechus* and as a *chov*.

blocks.question: How can one say that within *chesed* of *chachma* a person thinks the man is innocent and still finds a little bit of *chov*? Seemingly *chesed* of *chachma* should turn everything into a *zechus*, and each side should turn everything over to its side.
blocks.text: The answer: **that type of flipping only happens when you're in the etzem midda, which does not have hischalkus yet**. Only the *etzem hamidda* (the essence of the attribute), before any *hischalkus* (division), turns every point over to its own side.

But in *hischalkus* there can be *din* (judgement) in *chesed* of *chachma* and *chesed* in *din* of *chachma*. It depends whether you are talking on the level of the *nekuda* or the level of a *sefira*. In the *etzem*, just the *nekuda* of it, where there is no *hischalkus* yet, there can already be a kind of *chesed* of *chachma*; as was explained in chapter 17 about the *igulim* (circles), there is already a kind of division there, like a bribe, a *shochad*. But it is not a recognizable division, because it is really just a bias, and so it turns everything to its side.

blocks.title: The bribed judge
blocks.text:
When you are dealing with something that connects to the *etzem hamidda*, he is never going to compromise on it; it turns everything to its side. But once you come outside of the *etzem hamidda*, it is different. Say a person was bribed, so he has an *etzem midda* to make this guy innocent, and he is definitely going to make him innocent. But once he is making him innocent, he is being paid just to let the guy off. He does not really care whether the guy gets off and looks like a hero or not; he was not paid for that. Once it is outside the *etzem*, he can do it however he wants.

That is the idea of *hispashtus* (spreading forth): it is just the means to the end, not the goal itself. The *etzem hamidda* is connected to the goal itself. Once you are dealing with the means to an end, the *hispashtus* of the *midda*, you can compromise a little and say, "Well, it's true that he may not be whatever, but I still think he's innocent." So there can be different shades of *hiskalelus*.

This parenthesis is also a type of *hiskalelus*: the way there is a *hiskalelus* in the *nekuda*, in the *etzem midda*. But that is not called a *hischalkus nikeres*, a recognizable division, and so we do not usually speak of divisions there, even though you could make all these little divisions there too; they are all still in a *nekuda*. So it is not really what this chapter discusses, and that is why it is in parentheses. Here we discuss it as it comes out more, the *hispashtus*: the way of *sefira* and *partzuf*, the way it comes out from the *etzem nekuda*.

phrases.en: and similarly, that was in the *midda* of *chesed* of *chachma*, but the same would apply to the *middos* themselves, the actual feeling of love and the feeling of hate, for example.

blocks.text: That was in the *midda* of *chesed* of *chachma*, **but the same would apply to the middos themselves, the actual feeling of love and the feeling of hate.** **The chesed itself divides into a Keser, chachma, bina and middos**: a person has the intellect and everything for the *chesed*, and different emotions in the *chesed*, including *gevura*. And in *din* too there is the *sechel* (intellect) and the *middos* within the *din*.

*Ein merachamin badin*: **even though that when you're judging you're not allowed to have mercy, there can be no mercy in judgment.** So seemingly within a *midda* there is nothing of the opposite *midda*, and within love there is no *din*. The answer: **this is only in the essential din.** If you are dealing with the *etzem midda*, there will not be any *hiskalelus* of the opposite. But when you are dealing with its *hispashtus*, you can have different combinations.

blocks.title: The judge and the first-time offense
blocks.text: A judge has to judge objectively. He cannot get emotionally involved and feel bad; just because the person breaks down crying, he cannot change his judgment. He cannot have mercy like that. That is in the *etzem* of the judgment. But when it comes to the way he judges him, it could be a first-time offense or whatever; there are different reasons why they will not give him the maximum sentence. The law itself allows for different levels of guilt, and that is the idea of the different *middos* within it.

**So too there's no din in chesed atzmi**, in the essential *chesed*. **But when they spread out, from the essence**, there is *chesed* in *din* and *din* in *chesed*: then you can have this type of *hiskalelus*.

sections.title: The first kind: a thing nullified in its opposite, because the opposite is hidden in it
sections.summary: One kind of *hiskalelus* is *bittul* (nullification): the prosecutor becomes the defender, sugar overpowers cocoa, the merit itself becomes guilt. It is possible only because each side has its opposite hidden in it, as fire has something of water and *chesed* has a limit; without that, nothing would ever be included in its opposite.

phrases.he: והנה יש התכללות שנקרא ביטול דבר בהיפוכו המנגדו, והיה כמוהו ממש
phrases.en: There is one type of inclusion which is called the nullification of something in its opposite that opposes it, to the point where it becomes like it *mamash*, it becomes literally like it.
like the sweetening of severities in kindnesses
like the prosecutor gets transformed into a defender.
And also the opposite, when the defender gets turned over to a prosecutor.

blocks.text:
We just finished saying how each *sefira* divides into ten and subdivides into ten within each of those ten, with some examples. Now come the different types of *hiskalelus*.

**There is one type of inclusion which is called the nullification of something in its opposite that opposes it, to the point where it becomes like it mamash** (actually, literally): it gets totally turned over. It is **like the sweetening of severities in kindnesses**, **like the prosecutor gets transformed into a defender. And also the opposite, when the defender gets turned over to a prosecutor.**

This can also mean that the person himself gets won over. And when the person himself is won over, in a way it is even stronger, because he was on the other side. It lends strength.

blocks.title: The fighter against Chabad
blocks.text: Somebody was originally a big adversary, against something, and then he himself becomes pro. Say somebody was a big fighter against *Chabad*, and then he himself admits that it is right and true and becomes *Chabad*. That is a big help to the *Chabad* publicity and everything. Not only does it take away opposition; if even he admits it, it gives a boost to the defense.

That is why it would have been a big deal if the *Alter Rebbe* (Rabbi Schneur Zalman of Liadi) had met with the Gra, the Vilna Gaon. A big part of the opposition was based on the Gra, or at least was in his name, even if it was not really from him. If the Gra had met the *Alter Rebbe*, realized that it is a good thing and been pro, it would have dissolved a lot of the opposition.

phrases.en: or like the sweetening of bitter waters in sweet waters
or the opposite

blocks.title: Cocoa, coffee and sugar
blocks.text:
The same goes the other way, when a defender becomes a *mekatreg*. **Or like the sweetening of bitter waters in sweet waters**: take chocolate and put in sugar. Cocoa is very bitter, but if you put in a lot of sugar it becomes sweet. Coffee is very bitter too; add a lot of sugar and it is not as sweet as chocolate, but it also sweetens. Or lemonade, or anything like that. There the bitterness is totally nullified; now it actually becomes sweet, and it just tastes good.

**Or the opposite**: nullify the sweetness in bitterness, and then it just tastes bad. Taste something sweet with a lot of bitter things put in it and you will just taste bitter. It will taste worse than something that is just plain bitter, because in a way the contrast makes it more noticeable.

phrases.he: וכן ביטול שכל לזכות בשכל לחוב
phrases.en: and the same thing when an intellect for merit gets nullified in an intellect for guilt

blocks.text: **And the same thing when an intellect for merit gets nullified in an intellect for guilt.** That is what was said in the parenthesis before: when the merit is looked at from *din*, it gets totally turned over and the merit itself becomes a *din*.

blocks.title: The murderer's childhood, turned over
blocks.text: You are saying, "Well, you should let the person off. Look at his childhood and his surroundings and everything. If somebody else were in that situation he would also come to that, so he's not really worse than you." That is the merit: because he had such bad parents, such bad friends, and his whole environment and upbringing were so bad, it is not really his fault. But in *din* they say, "Yeah, but the fact that he was raised from the beginning in such a bad environment means that he's bad through and through. So for sure he's a danger to have around society, and there's no hope for us to try to reform him. He's totally rotten. Even though he has our sympathies, we should throw the book at him." So the merit itself gets turned over to a *chov*.

blocks.title: Rochel buried by the road
blocks.text: Or the opposite way, as in the *sicha* (talk) about *Rochel Imeinu*. Yaakov said to Yosef, "*Yesh b'libcha alai*": Yosef felt bad that his mother was not buried in the *Meoras HaMachpela*. And the answer Yaakov gave him turned it around into a *zechus*. The whole *inyan* of Rochel was having *mesirus nefesh* (self-sacrifice) to help other people. What she really wanted was to give away her place in the *Meoras HaMachpela* in order to be on the roadside to help the Jews, to *daven* for them. So the fact that she gives something up itself brings out the virtue of her *mesirus nefesh*, which was her main virtue, her main *avoda*. The main thing that turns it over is that she chose it, that it is something she would want. So what looked like her losing out becomes a bigger *zechus*.

phrases.en: This is a true inclusion.

phrases.he: והיינו רק לפי שיש כח זה במנגד עצמו
phrases.en: And the reason why this is possible is because there really is the other in the *menaged*, in the opposite side, there is hidden the other side also.

blocks.text: **This is a true inclusion**: here the one side totally loses its *metzius* (existence) and becomes the opposite. It is a complete *bittul* (nullification) of the opposite side; it is gone, and there is only one side now. **And the reason why this is possible is because there really is the other in the menaged, in the opposite side, there is hidden the other side also.**

Every person who opposes something has a little part of him that would go for it, that would be able to believe it, enjoy it and be into it. In a way, when a person has violent opposition, that shows he is very scared of letting that side out, and so he opposes it violently and forcefully to protect himself from it. That does not mean he is wrong; he could be protecting himself from something that really is bad. But if somebody does not feel threatened by it, it means he does not feel the part of him that would want it or be drawn to it, and so he will not run away from it so badly.

This is the difference between somebody who never sinned and a *baal teshuva* (a returnee to Judaism). Somebody who never sinned is supposed to say, "I want it, but what can I do? G-d told me not to." He is not in touch with the side of him that has a desire for these bad things, because he never tasted it. So he thinks that he is above it, that he has no desire and would never want it; he looks down on people who are involved in bad things and thinks they are just so bad, but he would never do it. To protect himself, he needs to acknowledge, "I really would want it, but G-d told me not to, so I'm not doing it." As soon as he starts thinking that he really does not want it, he is in trouble.

blocks.title: Adam thought he was a Rebbe
blocks.text: That was *Adam HaRishon*'s mistake. It says in *Likkutei Dibburim* that he thought he was a Rebbe, totally above the bad, and so he thought he could look at it and elevate it. But really he had a *yetzer hara* (evil inclination) for it, and by looking at it, it drew him into it and made him want it. He did not have an actual desire for it yet, because he had never tasted it; that is why it says the *yetzer hara* was outside of him. By looking at it, it connected him to it.

But the Maggid says that a *baal teshuva* should not say that. He should not say, "I want it, but G-d told me not to." He should say, "I don't want it," because he needs a bigger guard against going into it. Why? Because he already tasted it, so he knows that he has a desire for it; he does not need to admit that. He is able to say, "Yeah, I want it," and he knows it, but at the same time he has to say, "That whole desire and the pleasure and everything that comes along with it: I know I could enjoy it, but I don't want it." He is not saying that he cannot enjoy it; the *tzaddik* thinks he cannot enjoy it. The *baal teshuva* knows he can enjoy it, but he has to say that he does not want it. He has to totally hate it and go away from it, to protect himself from going back. And this is because he has this opposite side in him too.

then it would not be able to be nullified and included within it.

blocks.text: **And if it wasn't so, if it didn't have the opposite in it, then it would not be able to be nullified and included within it.** **For example, in something that's sweet, there is a hidden bitterness**; otherwise it could not be made bitter. **And in the bitterness there is a hidden sweetness.**

blocks.title: Honey and radish sauce
blocks.text: Like we see in a *mashal* and a *dimyon* (a likeness), **where you cook a sauce from honey and radishes, make a sweet and sour sauce.** **There you taste it's a delicious mixture of sharpness and sweetness together.** It brings out the sharpness in the sweetness and the sweetness in the sharpness, so you can taste how each one has both, and it is a good flavor. But add more of one or the other and it tips the other way, and you will taste only one. Even the radish has a certain sweetness in it, and if you put in enough sugar you will taste only the sweetness. And the other way: add enough radish and you will taste only the bitterness. Even sugar has a certain bitterness; especially the aftertaste of sugar is bitter. Something very sweet has a bitter taste to it. **As is known.**

phrases.en: similarly,

phrases.he: יש מטבע האש במים וממים באש
phrases.en: There is something of the nature, the characteristics of fire within water, and something of the characteristics of water within fire.

phrases.he: על כן יתכלל אש במים או מים באש
phrases.en: Therefore, you can have a mixture where fire and water, or water from fire, will combine with each other.
like it says in *Sefer Yetzira*,

phrases.en: Take out water from fire and fire from water,

blocks.text: **Similarly, there is something of the nature, the characteristics of fire within water, and something of the characteristics of water within fire.** This is talking about actual physical fire and water, and once you have physical fire and water you never have a pure *yesod* (element). You never have the pure thing of fire. Even what we call fire and water are not the four *yesodos* themselves: the real *yesod* of fire has no water in it, but everything in the physical world is a combination. So in physical fire and water there is always a combination.

blocks.title: Lightning from clouds, water from rocket fuel
blocks.text: From water you can have fire: lightning comes out of clouds of water, so in the water itself fire is really hidden. There are electrons, it can become ionized and bring out fire, like a flint can bring out fire. And fire can bring out water. First of all, a flame is kind of liquidy; it sticks to itself and has a certain moisture to it. Also, a lot of times a fire makes water: if you burn oxygen and hydrogen, it makes water. When the spaceship exploded on its way up ("which one, was it Challenger"), it made a cloud of water, because the rocket fuel is hydrogen and oxygen, and when it explodes it turns into H2O. And there are other ways that they are similar.

The idea of water is that it is wet and cold. So fire has a certain wetness to it, in that it sticks together; and even physical fire is not totally hot. The flame of a candle is only so hot; it is a relative heat. The same with water: the whole thing of water is that it is cold and wet, but there is still a certain warmth in water, it is not frozen. And it has a certain dryness: even though it generally sticks together, it does not totally stick together. The molecules stay apart from each other a certain amount, and different things like that.

**Therefore, you can have a mixture where fire and water, or water from fire, will combine with each other**, **like it says in Sefer Yetzira**: "**Take out water from fire and fire from water.**" That is what was just said: you can take water out of fire, since burning something sometimes produces water, and fire out of water, like lightning coming from water. Because one is included in the other, in the fire there is water and in the water there is fire.

phrases.en: so too with the emotions of *chesed* and *gevura*.

phrases.he: מפני שיש דין בחסד וחסד בדין כנזכר לעיל,
phrases.en: because there's always included a certain *din* within *chesed* and a certain *chesed* within *din*.

phrases.he: יבוטל הדין בחסד או להיפוך החסד בדין
phrases.en: And therefore you can nullify the *din* in *chesed*, or the opposite, you can nullify the *chesed* within *din*.
and if it was not so, that there is the *chesed* in the *din*, and the *din* in the *chesed*,

phrases.he: לא היה מתכלל דבר בהיפוכו לעולם
phrases.en: Then it would never, one thing would never include within the other thing, they would never be able to unite and come together.

blocks.text: **So too with the emotions of chesed and gevura**: within the *chesed* there is *gevura*, and within the *gevura* there is *chesed*, **because there's always included a certain din within chesed and a certain chesed within din.** How is this? Besides what was explained before, there are two things. One is that *chesed* always has some limit to it. If you are going to be nice to this person, but only to a certain amount or only in a certain way, there is a certain limit to it, a certain *din*. And it means that if the person were different, you would not have the *chesed*.

blocks.title: Your own child, and his enemy
blocks.text: You are kind to them because, say, they did something for you; but if they started being really bad, you would not have the *chesed* for them. Or even if you say it is an unconditional *chesed*, it is only because, say, it is your child: no matter what he does, you will still have *chesed* for him. But it is still only because it is your child, so for somebody else it would be *din*. And that is the other thing: a *chesed* for one person is a lot of times a *din* for somebody else. If you are going to be nice to this person and defend him against somebody else, you have a *din* for the other person, his enemy.

In the same way there is *chesed* in *din*. The whole premise of *din* is that this thing is bad. Why is it bad? Because you want to be good to something else. The main thing of justice is to punish. There is also reward, but in a regular government the main point of the justice system is not to reward people for doing good things; it is mainly to punish people, to stop them from doing bad things. The whole premise of that, though, is that you want to uphold society, for the betterment of the people. So in a way the main thing of justice is a *chesed*: you are trying to help people. And on the other hand, if you have a *chesed* and want to help people, automatically you have a certain *din*: you want to stop the bad things that will destroy what you love.

**And therefore you can nullify the din in chesed, or the opposite, you can nullify the chesed within din.** Say you have a *din*: by the letter of the law something is bad, but if you go and fight it you are going to destroy the whole thing that you love. Then the *din* goes away in the *chesed*, because the *chesed* is more powerful than the *din*. Or the opposite, the *chesed* goes into the *din*: if being nice is going to destroy the thing you love, you are going to want to go to *din*. Or there is something you like about a thing, but the bad things totally outweigh it, and it goes to *din*. Somebody does something nice for you, but then does so many bad things that it is overpowered in *din*; the merit is totally outweighed.

**And if it was not so, that there is the chesed in the din, and the din in the chesed, then it would never, one thing would never include within the other thing, they would never be able to unite and come together.**

So that is the one type of *hiskalelus*: one thing gets totally transformed by the other, totally *batel* (nullified) in it. This type is called *hiskalelus* in the thing itself, in the light itself. Within the light of *chachma* you can have *chesed* and *gevura*, and within those, *chesed* of *chesed* and *gevura* of *chesed*. And there are two kinds of *bittul* there. In one it is totally transformed into the opposite: the *chesed* becomes a *gevura*, the *gevura* becomes a *chesed*. In the other it does not become totally the opposite; it tempers it. Like what was said, "Well, the person's innocent, but not a total *tzaddik*." Within the *chesed* that is a *gevura* of *chesed*: the regular *hiskalelus* is that the *gevura* does not totally become a *chesed*, but within the *chesed* it is a little to the side of *gevura*, while still mainly on the side of *chesed*.

And it is like the difference between *nekuda*, *sefira* and *partzuf*. In the *etzem hamidda*, which is like a *nekuda*, everything is totally on one side. On that level even the *gevura* gets turned over into a *chesed*, and there is only *chesed* there: the argument that the person is innocent gets turned totally into a *zechus*, with no room for the other side. That is the idea of a bias, which just twists everything to its side. Then it spreads out like a *sefira*, and it already has differentiation: there is a *chesed* and a *gevura* and different shades, but it is all within the realm of *chesed*. That is the person who will acknowledge, "Okay, it's not totally good, but it's still better than anything else." The final point, that it is good, is not compromised; they are willing to acknowledge differences and another side, but then they are *mevatel* it. They say it is *batel b'rov*, nullified in the majority, or in a thousand, or in sixty, or whatever.

sections.title: The second kind, light in a vessel: kindness that is the strongest judgment
sections.summary: The next division is the lights going into vessels, where the opposite does not fight but strengthens. *Chesed sheb'gevura* is a judgment done by way of kindness: feeding your hungry enemy, the spy, the raise before the firing, G-d paying His enemies in this world, the voice that destroyed Sancheirev's camp. That is the strongest *din* of all.

blocks.text: Now comes a third type of *hiskalelus*; the first two fall under the same general category. This third type is the idea of *partzuf*, when the *oros* (lights) come into *kelim* (vessels). That is where you can have the light of *chesed* in the *kli* of *gevura*.

blocks.text: By the way, in *Sefiras HaOmer*, when we count *chesed* of *chesed*, *gevura* of *chesed*, it says that all those *middos* we are counting are the *middos* of *bina*: *chesed* of *chesed* of *bina*, *chesed* of *gevura* of *bina*. And usually, unless it specifies otherwise, the first division into ten is talking about the division within the lights, and the next division is the lights going into vessels. That is why we usually divide into ten and then into a hundred, "*yud* and *yud* of *yud*", as he said. So the first division is within the light of *bina*, which itself has *chesed*, *gevura*, *tiferes*, *netzach*, *hod*, *yesod*, *Malchus*: those are the seven weeks, each week one *midda* within the light of *bina*. Then the particular days, the next division, are that light going into the vessel. *Chesed* of *chesed* means the light of *chesed* of *bina* going into the *kli* of *chesed*; *gevura* of *chesed* means the light of *chesed* of *bina* going into the *kli* of *gevura*, and so on.

Now the type where the light goes into the vessel. **There's another type of inclusion of din into chesed because they are inherently alike, and not that it loses its nature.** On the contrary: **not only does the din not oppose the chesed and need to be nullified by the chesed, but it actually helps the chesed, and it gives strength to the chesed.** **And nevertheless, it's still called gevura of chesed.** And **also the opposite, there is also the idea of chesed of gevura**, which gives strength to the *gevura* and the *din*.

blocks.title: No compromise, unlike sugar in cocoa
blocks.text: Here the *chesed* not only does not oppose the *gevura* and need to be nullified by it; when they come together, one does not even temper the other. It is not like adding sugar to cocoa. There it is true that the sugar overpowers the cocoa and makes the whole thing sweet if you add enough sugar, but it is a fight, and at the end of the day chocolate is not as sweet as plain sugar. There is a certain compromise there. It brings out the sweetness, so in a way it is better, but it is not really as sweet; it is not pure sweetness. Here there is no compromise. Not only is there no compromise, it actually strengthens it.

phrases.en: and the *inyan* is, as is known,
like it says in the *passuk*,

phrases.he: אם רעב שונאך האכילהו לחם, כי גחלים כו'
phrases.en: It says, if your enemy is hungry, feed him bread, because it's like coals for his soul.

blocks.text: **And the inyan is, as is known,** **like it says in the passuk**: "**If your enemy is hungry, feed him bread, because it's like coals for his soul.**" What is it saying? That sometimes the biggest *din* you can do to somebody, the worst thing you can do to a person, is to be nice to him. If your enemy is starving, the plain *pshat* is that having to take bread from you, having you support him, totally eats him up. In a way it is the worst thing for him.

There are deeper things it refers to, like your *yetzer hara*. If your *yetzer hara* is hungry, mainly to be a *yesh* (something; existence), to be bigger, feed it bread, which is Torah. Say to it: "Oh, don't worry, come, we'll make you a big *metzius*. We'll make you a rabbi, we'll teach you all this Torah; even better, we'll teach you the secrets, we'll teach you *Chassidus*, and we'll make you a big guy, you'll know everything." It thinks it is going to get all blown up, but really it destroys the *yetzer hara* totally, and it makes him do *teshuva*.

blocks.title: The spy
blocks.text: Another example is a spy. The spy acts nice and is friendly with the enemy, and that itself makes it the most powerful *din*, the worst enemy. The worst thing you can do is to be nice to a person, get buddy-buddy with him, know all his secrets, and then stab him in the back. It is the most treacherous thing, the biggest *gevura*, even though externally it seems like a *chesed*.

What this really is, is the light of *chesed* coming into the *kli* of *gevura*. And this is the reason it does not oppose it. Within the level of the light, *chesed* and *gevura* oppose each other; within the level of the *kli*, *chesed* and *gevura* oppose each other. But the light of *chesed* coming into a *kli* of *gevura* is not a contradiction. Not only is it not a contradiction; in a way it is the most powerful *kli* for it, because it is hidden.

blocks.title: The raise before the firing
blocks.text: Somebody he knew ("I think it was an Iranian") said that what they would do, if an employer had an employee he really hated, was not just fire him. First he would give him a raise. For a while they would give him a lot of money and tell him what a great worker he is and how much he is worth to the company. Then, after he got it into his head that he was this bigger guy and should be making a lot of money, and got used to having the extra money, they would fire him: "You know, really you're a great asset, but we just can't afford to have you." For the rest of his life he would not be happy taking less money, and it would be much harder for him to get a job, because he thinks he is worth more than he is. So in a way they totally ruined him.

blocks.text: **So in this kindness and good that he's doing for him, he's really doing a complete evil to him and complete judgment, din, judgment on him, to totally destroy his soul.** That is one of the things it says: if your enemy is starving and you feed him, it is not like being mean to him. If you were mean to him, he would not be judged so badly, because he is mean to you and you are mean to him. But the fact that you are nice back makes him the only bad one, and then he gets totally punished.

**Similarly it says that G-d pays his enemies, he gives them their reward in this world so that he'll be able to totally destroy them in the next.** By giving reward to the wicked in this world, it looks like He is being nice to them, but it is really a total *din*, because He is just totally finishing them off: the more opportunity they have to go after their bad things and destroy themselves, to the point where they are beyond repair.

blocks.title: Spoiling him to ruin him
blocks.text: If you really hated somebody... As it says, spare the rod and spoil the child: somebody who hates his son does not give him rebuke. If a person really wanted to ruin somebody, he would just spoil him, give him whatever he wants, money, whatever, especially if he were a little rotten already, and he would get into bad habits and sink until he is totally incapacitated. That would be the light of *gevura* in the *kli* of *chesed*. That *chesed* is really a total *din*.

**And this is like the case with any din and onesh, any sort of judgment or punishment that is done in a way of chesed, that the chesed is the way that they're being punished**: **this is the strongest din possible, and this is also called chesed sheb'gevura.** Before, when we spoke of *chesed sheb'gevura*, it meant something like, "Well, even though I hate him, I don't hate him so much, because there's some good to him": a compromise. Here it is not a compromise. It is the opposite: it is even stronger.

phrases.he: וכמו והשמיע יהו״ה את הוד קולו במחנה סנחרב
phrases.en: Like it says that *Hashem* made heard the glory of his voice in the camp of Sancheirev.

blocks.text: **Like it says that Hashem made heard the glory of his voice in the camp of Sancheirev.** Here He destroyed the camp of Sancheirev by giving them a big *gilui Elokus* (revelation of G-dliness). He killed them all with a big *gilui Elokus*, which is a big *chesed*; it even says this name *Havaya*, which is the name of *chesed*. But because it was too big a *gilui*, they were all *batel*, and they all died. So it was a way of doing a *din*. In a way it was the worst *din*, because it exposed their evil and showed that they really have no existence. Their whole thing is to oppose G-d, and G-d revealed that only He is the real, true *metzius*, and it totally destroyed their *metzius*.

sections.title: Gevura sheb'chesed: harshness that is the strongest kindness
sections.summary: The opposite is kindness done in the garment of judgment: rain in measured drops, a teacher who brings it down, afflictions of love, tough love, the harsh cure that G-d prepared before the blow. That is stronger than plain kindness, and it is why our world is a *gevura* of *chesed*, a challenge to overcome.

blocks.text: **And so too the opposite**: *gevura sheb'chesed*, **that the gevura of chesed is the strongest chesed.** **This is when the act of kindness is done in a way through a means of din, so that it'll be stronger.** It is like **the gevuros of the rain**, which come in a *tzimtzum* so that they can be drawn down in abundance. **So the rain comes in small drops, but the fact that the kindness is given out in little measured way, that is what allows a lot of rain to come.**

blocks.title: Drizzle before the heavy rain
blocks.text: If it rains too fast, first of all it floods. And second, the ground first needs to be lightly wetted by a drizzle for a few days; then, when the ground is moist, it can absorb heavy rain, which will really grow the plants. Sometimes in a drought there is no light rain for a long time and the ground becomes parched and very dry. Then even a few days of heavy, heavy rain will not be absorbed into the ground; it just runs off. The top layer of the ground gets muddy and slides off, because the ground became hard and cannot absorb the water properly. It is a waste.

phrases.he: וכמו צמצום אור השפע בכל מקום, כדי שיתקבל
phrases.en: And this is like the *tzimtzum* of the light when something is being given over in any place, anytime that it's being given over, that's being made small so that it'll be able to be received.

blocks.title: The teacher who brings it down
blocks.text: A teacher limits his intellect to explain it simply to the student. The more he limits it and brings it down to the student, the bigger the kindness: he is making it easier and more understandable. The less he does that, the less of a kindness he is doing. The whole reason you have the teacher is to bring it down to your level. If you wanted it on his level, you could read it from the book yourself; you could just go get some very advanced textbook and read it. The whole thing is that you want it brought down.

and like it says that a father that wants, that desires his son, that loves his son, he rebukes him.

blocks.title: The bridge with many arches
blocks.text: And the same thing, **the division of the 72 bridges.** A bridge that spans a big river has a whole bunch of arcs, with a bunch of pillars going into the ground, so it is like a whole bunch of small bridges attached. Dividing it up like that slows the water down; it calms it, so it can flow nicer. That is the idea of the light of *chesed* coming into a *kli* of *gevura*: the *chesed* comes out in a small, divided, limited way.

**And the same thing with afflictions of love**: when G-d gives somebody challenges, but it is really to bring out his inner potential and strength; or when somebody is harsh on somebody because he knows the other really has more potential and he wants to bring it out. And as it says, a father who desires his son, **that loves his son, he rebukes him.**

blocks.text: **There the kindness is done specifically through the garment of din.** Really it is a total *chesed*, but it is done by being tough and harsh and forceful, for the other's benefit. It is like taking a knife away from a child, or a doctor doing harsh treatments that are really for the person's benefit, any kind of tough love.

This really shows a stronger kindness: it is like **a stronger love than the actual kindness itself.** Just to be nice and give somebody lollipops and presents is not such a big *chesed*. If you really love the person, you are willing to do something mean for him, to be tough with him. If you just have an immature *chesed*, which is really for yourself, you want to be seen as kind and want them to feel that you love them, so you only do things that are outwardly kind, because you want them to realize that it is kindness. But if you really love them and really care that they should benefit, even if they think you are being mean, you will be willing to do things that are outwardly mean for their benefit. That shows it is the strongest love.

blocks.text: **Like it says that G-d made the cure before the makka** (the blow). With any sickness, affliction or problem, G-d always made the cure first, because the real thing He wants is the cure, because He really loves us. And as it says, **G-d hits us, afflicts us, and heals us.** **So if so, why did G-d make the problem?** If the whole thing is that He wanted to fix it, why make the affliction in the first place? **But through being healed, then he becomes stronger.** There is an expression: anything that does not kill you makes you stronger.

**Because the sickness is a harsh din, a harsh severity, and it's taken away through the din of chesed, which is like harsh treatment.** **That's healing through harsh things, the harsh medicines that are like dangerous to a healthy person, or different treatments and surgeries and things like that.**

phrases.he: וכהאי גוונא בכל מיתוק הדין, בשרשו דווקא,
phrases.en: and this is the idea with the sweetening of *din*: it is always in its source,
which is the *din* of *chesed*.

phrases.he: להיותו תוקפו של חסד, לגבור על הדין ולהמתיקו כו' ודי למבין.

blocks.text: **And this is the idea with the sweetening of din: it is always in its source, which is the din of chesed.** The real source of all *din* is in the *din* of *chesed*, and it is the strength of *chesed* to overpower the *din* and sweeten it. In other words, the real reason G-d made bad things in the world is as a challenge, so that we should overcome them.

blocks.title: Basketball with an opponent
blocks.text: When you are playing a game, it is not so much fun to play basketball by yourself, just practice and get the ball in the hoop. Okay, you practice, you get good at it, you can get it in the hoop; it is not such a big deal. But if you have somebody else opposing you, it is much harder to get it in, and then you enjoy it more; it is more of an accomplishment. It is a bigger *chesed* when you get it in. Since the biggest *chesed* is the *din* of *chesed*, when the *chesed* manages to come even though a challenge opposes it, you want the opposition, to make a challenge to overcome.

And that is the whole thing of our world. It says that our world is the idea of *din* of *chesed*: that we should overcome a challenge and have to do *avoda* (divine service). It says the world of *Tohu* was like *chesed* of *chesed*, and now the world of *Tikun* is *gevura* of *chesed*. Because it explains that there are different *shemitos*: it says we are in the second *shemita* of the first *yovel*. The first *yovel* is all *chesed*, and within that we are in the second *shemita*, which is *gevura* of *chesed*. The first *shemita* was *Tohu*, and then comes the second, *gevura* of *chesed*.

That is why the world is full of bad things happening, and evil people doing bad things who seem to succeed. It is a very dark, difficult, challenging world. It is like one of those video games where there is a bunch of bad guys and one good guy, and he somehow manages to dodge all the bullets and kill all the bad guys and win. That is what it is like: the odds are way against us, in a way. But that in a way is the biggest thing: it is such a big challenge, and yet we are able to do it. It is a big *chiddush*.

That is what it says about our world: "*Zos chukas haTorah*." What is the idea of the *para aduma* (the red heifer)? That to make one person pure you have to make somebody else impure. The question is, why does the *chesed* have to come through a *din*? Why does there have to be a sacrifice to accomplish the goal? It is a *yerida l'tzorech aliya* (a descent for the sake of an ascent), but why does it have to be a *yerida*? So it says, "This is the *chok* of the Torah": that is the one *chok* (a commandment done just because G-d said so), because that is the whole thing of our world, that it is like that. Not just like the decree where G-d said, "*Shtok*, *kach ala b'ratzoni*": that's the way I wanted to make the world, and if you don't like it, too bad.

sections.title: Both at once: a light in a vessel is no contradiction
sections.summary: *Gevura sheb'chesed* and *chesed sheb'gevura* are the two greatest opposites, and yet they can come together, because each already shows two opposites: what it does and what it is inside. A light in a vessel is like matter and form, red ink spelling "green"; so Gavriel saved Avraham with fire, Avraham bound Yitzchak, and the Levi'im served the Kohanim.

phrases.en: So based on all this, it's understood the different ways that *chesed* and *gevura* can come together.
like *gevura* of *chesed*,
with, and that can unite with *chesed* of *gevura*,
even though they're two polar opposites seemingly, to their total opposites,

phrases.he: שזה תוקף החסד וזה תוקף בגבורה
phrases.en: that one is the forcefulness and the strength of *chesed*, the other one is the forcefulness and the strength of *gevura*,

phrases.he: ומכל שכן מצד התפשטות לבושים מחולפים,
phrases.en: and especially because of they switched, when you look at the garments which are switched,

phrases.he: שזה פועל דין וזה פועל חסד
phrases.en: that one is just when you look at the most external thing of what's going on, one is *din* and one is *chesed*.

blocks.text:
**So based on all this, it's understood the different ways that chesed and gevura can come together.** You can have *chesed* of *gevura* in the light, and then the *ha'ara* (glow) of *chesed* going into the *kli* of *gevura*; you can keep dividing more and more in the light, and more and more in the vessel. Once you have all these types of *hiskalelus*, you can even have *gevura sheb'chesed*, **like gevura of chesed**, the light of *chesed* going into the *kli* of *gevura*, like a parent's love going into strictness, **unite with chesed of gevura**, like the spy, where the light of *gevura*, the hatred, comes out being nice.

**Even though they're two polar opposites seemingly**: **one is the forcefulness and the strength of chesed, the other one is the forcefulness and the strength of gevura.** And especially **when you look at the garments which are switched**: looking at the most external thing that is going on, **one is din and one is chesed.** In this case the parent is expressing *din*, and the spy is expressing *chesed*.

phrases.en: nevertheless,

phrases.he: מצד שכל אחד פועל בשביל דבר היפוכו דוקא,
phrases.en: since each one is *poel* for the opposite,
that the *gevura* of *chesed*, which like a parent that is being strict and harsh with his son, the effect, the external thing is *din*, that he's being harsh,
but the real *pnimiyus*, the real intention is *chesed*, is kindness,
and the kindness within *gevura*, in other words the light of *gevura* going into the *kli* of *chesed*,
externally it's nice, it's being kind,
but the real thing inside of it is *din*, is harshness,

phrases.he: על כן יוכלו לבוא כאחד דוקא,
phrases.en: therefore they can come together at once

phrases.he: מפני שכל אחד מראה ב' הפכים על כל פנים
phrases.en: because each one has two opposites.

blocks.text: **Nevertheless, since each one is poel** (works) **for the opposite**: in *gevura* of *chesed*, like a parent who is strict and harsh with his son, **the effect, the external thing is din, that he's being harsh, but the real pnimiyus, the real intention is chesed, is kindness.** And *chesed* of *gevura*, **the light of gevura going into the kli of chesed**: **externally it's nice, it's being kind, but the real thing inside of it is din, is harshness.** **Therefore they can come together at once, because each one has two opposites.** Since each one has two opposites, you can really have both together. How is that possible?

blocks.title: The teacher, from both sides
blocks.text: When a teacher is teaching, the students are getting a *chesed*, because he is teaching them. But that *chesed* really comes from a *gevura*: he is limiting his *sechel*. So to the students the *chesed* comes out of a *gevura*, but to the teacher it is the opposite. For him it is really a *gevura*, that he is limiting himself; but really it is a *chesed*, because he is being kind.
It is like this: whenever you face somebody, your right hand is on his left side and your left hand is on his right side. It is opposites.

blocks.title: The spy who loves his country
blocks.text: When the spy is nice to them and has a *chesed* for them, it is externally a *chesed*, and really he is doing it to destroy the other side; and at the same time it is really also a *gevura* of *chesed*. For the enemy he is doing *chesed* of *gevura*, being nice in order to destroy them. But it is really *gevura* of *chesed*, because he loves his country, which is a *chesed*, and he is willing to go against what he likes to do and help the enemy, which is a *gevura*. He totally hides his true self and his patriotic feelings for his country and goes and hangs out with the enemy, which for him is a big *gevura*. So which is it, *gevura* of *chesed* or *chesed* of *gevura*? It is really both, *davka* at the same time. What is *chesed* for one thing is *gevura* for the other, and even in the external effect, what is *chesed* for one is *gevura* for the other. So not only is it possible to have both together; in a way you always have them both together.

phrases.en: Like it says that Gavriel was sent that he saved Avraham.
and it says he cooled down the coals, that he made them not as hot,
So this is the idea of *gevura* of *chesed*,

blocks.title: Avraham in the furnace
blocks.text:
**Like it says that Gavriel was sent that he saved Avraham.** When Avraham was thrown into the *kivshan ha'eish*, the fiery furnace, it says Gavriel wanted to save him, but G-d said that since he is one in the world, "I'm going to save him Myself." Since Gavriel had wanted to save him, later he got to save Chananya, Mishael and Azarya. And it says that first the *malach* (angel) of *chesed* wanted to save him: "Let me come make it rain or snow, and I'll put out the fire of the furnace." Then Gavriel said, "No, let me save him; it'll be more of a *chiddush* if he'll be saved through *gevura*."

So it could be that it was still in a way done through Gavriel, but since it was done with two opposites at the same time, it was as if G-d Himself did it; it shows that it comes from G-d. Avraham was in the fire, and G-d made the fire even stronger, so that it burned the people who threw him in; it killed them because it was so hot. And at the same time, for him it was not hot. He was walking around there and he was cool.

And he cooled down the coals: at a different time Gavriel was sent to destroy a town and pour the coals on them, and it says **he cooled down the coals, that he made them not as hot**, because he did not want just to destroy it. **So this is the idea of gevura of chesed**: he was doing a *chesed*, saving Avraham, through *gevura*, through the fire.

phrases.he: כמו זיעה טובה מוציא את חולי החום,
phrases.en: like a good sweat that takes out the sickness,
or like a medicine for some affliction, which is specifically like a harsh treatment.
and yet it says that Gavriel was the same one that hit *machane* Sancheirev,
which that is *chesed* of *gevura*.

phrases.he: כמו שכתוב ויצא מלאך יהו״ה כו'
phrases.en: that he is called *malach Hashem*, a *malach* of kindness, because it was really the *chesed* of *gevura*.

blocks.text: **Like a good sweat that takes out the sickness**: sometimes when a person is sick, even with a fever, it helps to wrap him and make him hotter, so that he sweats, and that helps take away the fever. **Or like a medicine for some affliction, which is specifically like a harsh treatment.**

sensitivity.reason: Says that wrapping a sick person who has a fever to make him hotter helps take the fever away, which a reader could act on as medical advice.
sensitivity.publishable: **Like a good sweat that takes out the sickness**, **or like a medicine for some affliction, which is specifically like a harsh treatment.**

blocks.text: **And yet it says that Gavriel was the same one that hit machane Sancheirev**, the camp of Sancheirev, which is **chesed of gevura**: as it says, "And the *malach* of *Havaya* went out", **he is called malach Hashem, a malach of kindness, because it was really the chesed of gevura.** The *gevura*, the severity, happened through *chesed*, through a big *gilui*. The reason it could be done that way ("as is known, *v'dai l'mevin*") is that for Sancheirev it was done in a way of *chesed* of *gevura*, but for the Jews it was really a *gevura*, a *gevura* against their enemy. So the *malach* of *gevura* was able to go and punish them that way, even though externally it is a thing of *chesed*. A *malach* cannot do two opposite things, but this is not considered two opposite things; it is considered the same thing.

phrases.he: והיינו לאכללא שמאלא בימינא וימינא בשמאלא
phrases.en: This is what it means to include the left in the right and the right in the left.

phrases.he: שהוא כמו אור החסד בכלי הגבורה,
phrases.en: This is the idea, the light of *chesed* going into *kli hagevura*,
that the vessel does the opposite of its light.

phrases.he: שכלי הגבורה פועל דין, היפוך אור של חסד שבו
phrases.en: that the vessel of *gevura* affects *din* externally, which is the opposite of the light of *chesed* in it.

phrases.he: וכן להיפוך, כלי החסד פועל חסד, היפוך אור הגבורה שבו
phrases.en: In the same way, the vessel of kindness affects externally a kindness, which is the opposite of the light of *gevura* that is in it.

blocks.text: **This is what it means to include the left in the right and the right in the left.** **This is the idea, the light of chesed going into kli hagevura, that the vessel does the opposite of its light**: **the vessel of gevura affects din externally, which is the opposite of the light of chesed in it.** Like a parent who is strict: the vessel is *din*, and that is the way he shows the love. **In the same way, the vessel of kindness affects externally a kindness, which is the opposite of the light of gevura that is in it.**

phrases.en: but this is really not an opposite at all,
because it's a light in the vessel,
which the idea of the light in the vessel is like a *chomer* and a *tzura*, the matter and the form.

blocks.text: **But this is really not an opposite at all, because it's a light in the vessel**, and there is no contradiction in your light being *chesed* and your *kli* being *gevura*. As long as it is good for him, you do not care how it is done or which *kli* you use. Whatever gets the job done. **The idea of the light in the vessel is like a chomer and a tzura, the matter and the form**: *chomer v'tzura*.

blocks.title: Red ink that spells "green"
blocks.text: Take a red pen and write the word "green". If I ask you, "Is it red or is it green?", you say it depends what you mean: the ink is red, but the form spells green. Is it a contradiction? No, not at all. One is the *chomer*, one is the *tzura*. You can take black ink and write the word "white", and white ink and write the word "black", and it does not contradict at all. The same way, you can take a vessel of *gevura* and make it into a *chesed*, and take the vessel of *chesed* and make it into a *gevura*, and it is not a contradiction at all, because you are just using it for that purpose. Your goal and the means you use to accomplish it are totally independent.

phrases.he: וכמו שכתוב במקום אחר בענין התכללות דשם מ''ב ושם ע''ב,
phrases.en: as it is explained elsewhere about the inclusion of the name of 42 with the name of 72,

phrases.he: שהן ב' פרשיות דקריאת שמע כו'
phrases.en: which these are the two *parshiyos* of Shema.

blocks.text: **As it is explained elsewhere about the inclusion of the name of 42 with the name of 72, which these are the two parshiyos of Shema.** In the first *parsha* of *Shema*, *V'ahavta*, there are 42 words. The name of 42 is the name of *Ana B'choach*: there are 42 words in *Ana B'choach*, and the initials spell out those names on the side, a 42-letter name of G-d. That is the name of *gevura*, the idea of *aliya*, from below upward. Then the name *Ayin Beis*, 72, is the *gematria* of *chesed*.

"I don't think this refers to the famous *Shem Ayin Beis*, which is *chachma*." He thinks it refers to a different *Shem Ayin Beis*; more than one thing has a *gematria* of 72. This *Shem Ayin Beis* is a name of *chesed*, the idea of *hamshacha* (drawing down) from above to below. The first *parsha* of *Shema* starts right away with *V'ahavta*, a thing of *chesed*, a big *gilui*, talking about a person on the level of a *tzaddik*. But this big *gilui* from above and this big love cause the idea of the 42, a burning desire to go up to G-d, which is a *gevura*. So you have the *chesed* and *gevura* together.

In the second *parsha* of *Shema* there are 72 words, from *V'haya im shamoa* until *v'samtem*, including *v'samtem*: that is the name of 72, the name of *chesed*. But if you read the *parsha*, it says that if you are not going to listen, all these bad things will happen. It is talking about a person who is not on such a high level and does not have this big love for G-d, and there is not such a big *gilui*, which is a thing of *gevura*. But really its purpose, as was said, is that the challenge should bring out the *chesed*, and in a way it reveals a deeper *chesed*.

So sometimes it says that the first *parsha* is the light of *chesed* in the *kli* of *gevura*, and sometimes that it is the light of *gevura* in the *kli* of *chesed*; and the same with the second *parsha*. And the *Tzemach Tzedek* explains in *Derech Mitzvosecha*, *Shoresh Mitzvas HaTefilla*, that the *shem* (the name) is a *memutza* (a middle) between the *or* and the *kli*, and he explains how it is both.

phrases.he: וכמו עקידת יצחק באברהם, איש החסד
phrases.en: and similarly, like *Akeidas Yitzchak*, which was done by Avraham, which is *ish hachesed*.

blocks.text: **And similarly, like Akeidas Yitzchak, which was done by Avraham, which is ish hachesed** (the man of kindness). How can Avraham go and be willing to sacrifice his son? That is such a *gevura*! The reason is that the real thing of Avraham's *chesed* is for G-d: he loved G-d, and whatever is G-dly is a good thing to him. So if that is accomplished through a *gevura*, it is not a problem. It is no contradiction at all that Avraham should do something externally *gevura*, because if G-d said to do it, then it is a *chesed*. It is a good thing.

phrases.en: or like the Levi'im, when the Levi'im were given instead of the *bechorim* to help the Kohanim, so it says that they were waved, the Levi'im were waved, and they were given over to the Kohanim.
like it says that they will take them to you.
How can they serve the opposite?
and there's many examples of this.

blocks.text: **Or like the Levi'im, when the Levi'im were given instead of the bechorim** (the firstborn) **to help the Kohanim**: it says that they were waved, **and they were given over to the Kohanim.** But the Kohanim are *chesed*, so how can the Kohanim be served by Levi'im, which are *gevura*? **Like it says** ("*V'yilavu alecha*") **that they will take them to you.** **How can they serve the opposite?** **And there's many examples of this.**

sections.title: Because each is divided, each finds its kind in the other
sections.summary: All this works only once each *sefira* is divided into its own ten, the level of *partzuf*: then each finds its kind in its opposite and wakes up, like milk that returns in meat. So Michael and Gavriel, fire and water, do not put each other out, and peace comes from separating the light, the goal, from the vessel, the means.

phrases.he: וכל זה אינו רק מצד בחינת ההתחלקות שבכל אחד
phrases.en: and the reason that this is possible is because once you have the level of *partzuf*, once there's a complete *hischalkus* in each and every one, each *sefira* already has its own ten, and divides into ten, and ten into ten.

phrases.he: על כן מצא מין את מינו וניעור,
phrases.en: So then each thing finds its *min*, and it gets woken back up.

phrases.he: גם בהיותם ב' הפכים ממש כו'
phrases.en: even though they're two opposites,

blocks.text: **And the reason that this is possible is because once you have the level of partzuf, once there's a complete hischalkus in each and every one, each sefira already has its own ten, and divides into ten, and ten into ten.** Therefore *matza min es mino v'nei'or*: **each thing finds its min** (its kind), **and it gets woken back up.**

blocks.title: Milk that wakes up in meat
blocks.text: This is a thing in the laws of mixtures, and also in *Eruvin*; it is used in different cases where you have a mixture of opposites. Say a little bit of milk went into meat. If it is just a little, it is *batel*. But if you keep adding more drops, eventually the taste is going to come back and you will be able to taste the milk again, and then it is not *batel* anymore. *Matza min es mino*: the *min* finds its other *min*, and it wakes back up and becomes a *metzius* again.

So really, even though the Levi'im are externally mainly a thing of *gevura*, they really have a little *chesed* in them. When they connect to the Kohanim, the Kohanim bring out the *chesed* in the Levi'im and find a way to use the Levi'im to help them. And the Levi'im connect to the *gevura* in the Kohanim, and their connection to the Kohanim strengthens them too. So each one is really able to work together with the other, **even though they're two opposites**, because once they have *hischalkus* they can come together.

phrases.he: וכמו ענין התחלקות מיכאל וגבריאל, שר של אש ומים
phrases.en: like the divisions of Michael and Gavriel, which those are the angels of fire and water.

phrases.he: ואין מכבין זה את זה, כמו שכתוב עושה השלום כו'
phrases.en: nevertheless they do not extinguish each other, G-d makes peace *bimromav*, in the heavens he makes peace between *chesed* and *gevura*, between the *malachim* of *chesed* and *gevura*.

phrases.he: לפי שיש בכל אחד מהיפוכו המנגדו דוקא
phrases.en: since each one really has something of the opposite, so therefore they're able to come together.

blocks.text: **Like the divisions of Michael and Gavriel, which those are the angels of fire and water. Nevertheless they do not extinguish each other**, as it says, *oseh shalom*: **G-d makes peace bimromav, in the heavens he makes peace between chesed and gevura, between the malachim of chesed and gevura**, **since each one really has something of the opposite, so therefore they're able to come together.**

blocks.title: Democracy
blocks.text: This is like the idea of a democracy. Everybody has his own desires, and from the side of the light they do not agree. But when it comes to actually doing things, to the *kli*, they may be able to find some *kli* that I want because it will help me for this, and you want because it will help you for that, and then we are able to work together.

We ask the One who makes peace above to make peace below: "*Oseh shalom bimromav, Hu ya'aseh shalom aleinu*." The main peace is between G-d and the world, between G-dliness and the world, spiritual and physical. To make this peace, the main thing that has to happen is a *birur* (clarification): you have to separate everything, make a division, separate the light from the vessel, the goal from the means. First you clarify what your goal is, and the goal is to connect to G-d. And what is the means, which is not the goal? That is the physical world. So the first thing you have to do is purify your goal more and more.

The more you understand that your goal is not to connect to G-d in order to get *Gan Eden* or *Olam HaBa*, not even to be holy and close to Him, but just to do whatever G-d says, the highest, most pure goal. Once you refine that, you go back and look at the means: you look at everything in the world, the spiritual world and the physical world, and ask, how can I use this for this goal? Then you see that some things are good, like *tefillin*: *tefillin* are really good for a *mitzva*, so that becomes a good thing. But certain times it is not: on *Shabbos* you should not put on *tefillin*; or if it is a matter of danger to life, you should not say, "Oh, now I have to go put on *tefillin*." So the main source of peace is when you are able to separate the light and the vessel; then you see that they do not contradict, and you can have them both together.

That is the idea of *oseh shalom*: really there is already peace. Above there is already peace, because there the light and the vessels are properly divided and separated. By us there is no peace, because to us it is not *mevorar*, not clear: it is not clear what the real *kavana* (intention) is, what the real goal is, what the *or* is and what is only a *kli*. So we ask that it should come down to us. And that is why right after *oseh shalom* comes *yibaneh Beis HaMikdash*.

In the *Yehi ratzon* we ask to be given our portion in the Torah, because the Torah is what lets us have peace; the Torah makes peace in the world. And that is the main way it does it, because the main problem comes when somebody tells you, "Oh, this is good," and you do not realize what part of it is good and what part is not. You just take the whole thing as one package deal. But you have to see that the *or* is the real thing, and the *kli* you can change. "Because each one has something of its opposite *davka*."

sections.title: The points cannot combine, except through mesirus nefesh, which turns even the essential bad to good
sections.summary: In the simple lights, the *nekudos* called *Kesarim*, nothing combines: the depth of good and the depth of bad have no connection. Yet the *baal teshuva*'s sins become merits, through *mesirus nefesh* that reaches the Essence above *chesed* and *gevura*; there prayer can change the way G-d does things. The three kinds become three ways of *avoda*: trust past the vessel, a light that overpowers, and enjoying the challenge itself.

phrases.en: but in the lights, the way they're completely simple,
which this is a level of the *nekudos*, even before *sefira*,
which are called the crowns, the *Keser* of each *sefira*,
they cannot unite at all.

phrases.he: מפני שכל אחד נבדל לגמרי מזולתו,
phrases.en: because each one is completely separate from the other one,

phrases.he: ולא ימצא בו כלל מבחינת המנגדו
phrases.en: and you have nothing of the opposite.

phrases.he: כמו עצם בחינת הטוב שבעצמיות נפש איש הטוב, הנקרא עומק טוב,
phrases.en: like the essence of the goodness in the inner self, the inner soul of a good person, which is called the depth of good, his pleasure in being good,
with the essence of bad,
which is called the depth of bad.

blocks.text: **But in the lights, the way they're completely simple**, **a level of the nekudos, even before sefira**: first there is the light the way it is *pashut* (simple), the *nekuda*; then the light the way it divides, the *sefira*; and then the light the way it comes into a vessel, the *partzuf*. When you go all the way up to the first, the *nekudos* **which are called the crowns**, the *Kesarim*, **the Keser of each sefira**, **they cannot unite at all.** At that level there is no *hiskalelus*, **because each one is completely separate from the other one, and you have nothing of the opposite.**

It is **like the essence of the goodness in the inner self, the inner soul of a good person, which is called the depth of good, his pleasure in being good**, **with the essence of bad**, **which is called the depth of bad.** There is no connection between the two. One enjoys good and one enjoys bad, and they cannot unite. Maybe you could use the bad person for a good thing, but at the level of the ultimate goal they are opposites, and they cannot come together.

phrases.he: אך בבעלי תשובה אנו רואים שנהפך גם עצם הרע לטוב,
phrases.en: nevertheless, we do see a type of *hiskalelus*, this is the third type of *hiskalelus*, which is in the actual *etzem nekuda* itself, where the essence of the bad gets turned over to good.
And similarly, the sins themselves become merits.

phrases.he: הרי הוא מצד מסירת נפש בעצמות אור אין סוף,
phrases.en: This is only possible when a person reveals their *mesirus nefesh*, their connection to G-d Himself,

phrases.he: שלמעלה גם מהתחלקות עצם החסד וגבורה
phrases.en: which is higher than the division of *chesed* and *gevura*.

blocks.text: **Nevertheless, we do see a type of hiskalelus, this is the third type of hiskalelus, which is in the actual etzem nekuda itself, where the essence of the bad gets turned over to good**: in the *baal teshuva*. **And similarly, the sins themselves become merits**; they become *mitzvos*. **This is only possible when a person reveals their mesirus nefesh, their connection to G-d Himself, which is higher than the division of chesed and gevura.**

At that level, even the inner pleasure a person has in doing bad, the pleasure of rebelling against G-d and being his own *metzius*: if he goes to the real depth behind that depth, it is really a thing of revealing that there is only G-d. It just reveals how G-d could be *metzamtzem* (contract) Himself so much that it looks like a real *metzius*; but it is really a *gilui* of Him, a *gilui* of His power of *tzimtzum*. So it is really the same thing as the *chesed*, revealing that there is only G-d: even something that looks like a total opposite is also coming from Him. At that level, G-d is revealed through the *aveiros* (sins) and through the *mitzvos* equally.

*Lechatchila* we have to do it through the *mitzvos*, because G-d chose *mitzvos*, because G-d chose that *giluyim* (revelations) should be important. But at the level of the *etzem* it is there equally in both. The whole reason an *aveira* is an *aveira* is that a Jew is connected to G-d and G-d told him not to do it. So the fact that it is bad, and the whole feeling that it is bad, is itself a *gilui* of his connection to G-d; otherwise it would not be bad, it would not be a problem. It just reveals it in a negative way. But we do not want to reveal it in a negative way. Even though the *etzem* is the same, that he is a Jew and therefore connected to G-d, since G-d chose the *giluyim*, it is important that it be done in a good way.

Nevertheless, from the side of the *etzem*, they are both revealing G-d. So a person should not do *aveiros*; it is *mamash* a terrible thing. But once a person did it, it is possible to do *teshuva* and reveal something good in it.

phrases.he: ולכך יכולים במסירת נפש דווקא, להתפלל ולומר יהי רצון, בעצם, מלפניך כו'
phrases.en: And this is why specifically when a person has *mesirus nefesh* can they *daven* and ask G-d to change the way He does things.

blocks.text: **And this is why specifically when a person has mesirus nefesh can they daven and ask G-d to change the way He does things.** That is what it says: the secret of being answered in your prayers, in *Shemoneh Esreh*, is the *mesirus nefesh* you have in *Krias Shema* before it. When you reveal the level of *mesirus nefesh*, where you have an *etzem* connection to G-d, at that level *chesed* and *gevura* are the same. So at that level you can ask G-d to change the way He does things, because there it does not matter which way He does them. You can ask Him to make it different, because at that level He too has, as it were, *mesirus nefesh* for you, to do it the way you want it.

phrases.he: וכן ויעבור יהו״ה על פניו כו'
phrases.en: and this is also like it says that G-d passed over his face, in other words went past the *pnimiyus*, which is like the reason of the *sechel*.

phrases.he: וכמו שיתבאר בענין י''ג תקוני דיקנא כו' ודי למבין
