blocks.text: **And this is also like it says that G-d passed over his face, in other words went past the pnimiyus** (the inner side), **which is like the reason of the sechel.** And then He said the thirteen *middos harachamim* (attributes of mercy), *Kel rachum*, **to turn even the essential din into a chesed**: that is the idea of forgiving sins and turning the *zedonos* (willful sins) into *zechuyos* (merits). That is the idea of the thirteen *middos harachamim*, and it is possible when we connect to G-d in a way that is higher than the *sechel* and higher than the Torah.

blocks.title: Erase me from Your book
blocks.text: That is what Moshe said to G-d: "If You're not going to forgive them, *mecheini na*, erase me from Your book." The Rebbe explains that he wanted to go higher than the Torah: if You are not going to forgive them on the level of the Torah, let's go higher than the level of the Torah. And G-d told him, "The one that sins against Me, I will erase him from My book." In other words: "I prefer people that keep the Torah. I'd rather people keep the Torah and do things within the rules. If somebody's not going to do it within the rules, then I'll forgive them higher than the rules."

phrases.he: (והיינו על ידי בחינת הקו וחוט, שיש בו מכח עצמות אור אין סוף ממש
phrases.en: This is coming from the *Kav* and *chut*, which has in it the *koach* of G-d himself.

phrases.he: כמו שכתוב זכרונם לברכה אליו ולא למדותיו,
phrases.en: like our Sages taught us, we should pray to G-d and not to his *middos*.
and not even to his essential *middos*,

phrases.he: וכמו שיתבאר בעזרת השם ודי למבין):
phrases.en: like will be explained with the help of G-d, and this is sufficient for the understanding.

blocks.text: As it is explained about the thirteen *tikunei dikna*, the thirteen parts of the beard, "oh, and by the way", they will be explained in chapter 25, *im yirtzeh Hashem*. **This is coming from the Kav and chut, which has in it the koach of G-d himself.** In other words, the way things are measured out by the lines, they are measured out by G-d. It is like the teacher who decides how to set up the class and how it is going to work: he decides the rules. So since he makes the rules, he can break the rules.

**Like our Sages taught us**, *eilav v'lo l'middosav*: **we should pray to G-d and not to his middos, and not even to his essential middos**, **like will be explained with the help of G-d, and this is sufficient for the understanding.**

If you notice, it starts already now, or maybe a little before, and it is going to continue like this for a lot of the rest of the book: he does not clearly differentiate between the *mashal* and the *nimshal*. They are just kind of intertwined, and you have to work a little more to *chap* (catch) what the point of the *nimshal* is. The point is these three levels of *hiskalelus*: G-d can reveal any *or* through any *kli*, so we have to differentiate between the *or* and the *kli*. Later on there are going to be five chapters about *oros* and *kelim*, and there the *nimshal* of this will be clearer.

There is one type of *avoda*, the *avoda* of *emuna*: you trust that whatever G-d is doing is for the best, that G-d really loves you and is really doing good things for you. Even though the vessel can look like *gevura*, you trust that it is really a *chesed*, and so you are always happy and always faithful to G-d; you know He is always doing the best for you, and you are not worried. Do not be fooled by the external vessel of things. Sometimes something looks good and something bad comes from it; sometimes something looks bad and something good comes from it. The external way something looks has nothing to do with what is going to come from it; it is totally irrelevant. So you should not be fooled: as soon as something starts to look a little like this or a little like that, "Oh no!", or you get all excited, "Oh look, it's all good." You never know what can come from it.

That is also one of the reasons everything is in G-d's hands. G-d gives us a certain amount of *bechira* (free choice), and we can do whatever we want, but everything we do is only a vessel, and G-d can fill the vessel with whatever He wants. Even if you say, "All right, I made this great business deal, it's a foolproof *kli*", it is not true. It is impossible to make a *kli* that G-d cannot turn the opposite way if He wants to. So you have to have *emuna* in G-d that He can always make it turn out good, and you have to trust in Him. And you need His *bracha*, because if G-d does not bless your deeds, your vessel is meaningless, and it can even be turned over to the opposite.

Then there is another type of *hiskalelus*, in the *or* itself. Say you are already looking at *kedusha* (holiness) with *kavana*: some things reveal G-d more and some less. There the *or* of *kedusha* has to become so strong that it totally overpowers the light of the other side. In a person's *avoda*, his desire for bad things has to be totally overpowered by his desire and pleasure in good things; that has to be a very strong light. In the first way, the light and the vessel, even something that seems to oppose G-d is totally irrelevant; it does not oppose Him. That is like *bittul hayesh*: it can still have its *metzius*, and it is *batel*.

In a way this is a higher type of *bittul*, where G-d's *gilui* is so great that in front of it everything is *kula kamei k'lo chashiv*, everything else is irrelevant. That is the thing of a *tzaddik*: the *gilui* of G-d is so big that any opposition is totally blown away. It is true that G-d can make the bad turn out good, but you say, "Well, it's still painful, it's still difficult." A person has to realize that the little bit of difficulty and pain a person has in this world is totally nothing next to the good that comes from being able to do *mitzvos* and connect to G-d. You do not see it as a bad thing; the pleasure you have connecting to G-d totally outweighs it. It is a tiny nothing. At that level you do acknowledge that something is there, but it is totally irrelevant, as if *batel*.

Then there is an even higher thing, in the *etzem or*, the third type of *hiskalelus*. That is the *gilui hayechida* (the revelation of the essence of the soul), where even the bad itself becomes good. A person reveals his *mesirus nefesh* for G-d to the point where he not only feels it is worth suffering for G-d; he actually enjoys it. It is just another way of expressing his connection, a challenge or whatever, and it is not seen as something that opposes at all. That is the level of *ein od milvado* (there is nothing besides Him).

blocks.title: Playing the game
blocks.text: It is like a person who knows he is playing a game: there is a challenge and it is hard, but he does not feel that he is enduring a little pain to get something good. He chooses to do it; he enjoys it; he enjoys the challenge. And that is *pada v'shalom nafshi mikrav li*, "redeem my soul in peace from those that fight with me": there is something fighting him, *mikrav li*, and at the same time it is *pada v'shalom*. Why? Because when the *yechida* is revealed, even though there is opposition, you realize that the whole existence of that opposition is to make a challenge for you, and that itself is part of your *avoda*. So you do not see it as a real, opposite *metzius*. You see it as really part of your own *metzius*.

In a way it is similar to the first one. That is why *Tikun* is higher than *Tohu*: *Tikun* is the *hiskalelus* of the *or* in the *kli*, and *Tohu* is just the *hiskalelus* in the *or*. But the difference is that in the first one you really see it as bad, only something good can come out of it; you look at it as a means to an end, "Well, you can accomplish something good through this." Here, even as an end in itself, you enjoy the way you do it.

blocks.title: Winning the game or playing it
blocks.text: Say you are playing basketball. Do you enjoy winning the game, or do you actually enjoy playing the game? If you just enjoy winning, it is frustrating that there is an opposition to overcome, an opponent, and you are happy when you win. But if you have a more mature appreciation, you enjoy playing the game. You enjoy the process, and the challenge itself while you are doing it. So the difficulty itself becomes a good thing.

That is where a person realizes, even if it is not something he can totally feel, at least to be aware of it in thought, that from G-d's point of view He is creating the whole world from nothing, and from that point of view it is like a game or a story where nothing is a means to an end. You cannot say that something is just a *kli* to accomplish some purpose. That would be saying, "Really G-d wants the *aliya*, and the *yerida* is only for the *aliya*, but really G-d doesn't want the *yerida*." Then why did He make the *yerida*? G-d did not have to make the *yerida*; He could have made the *aliya* without the *yerida*. Rather we must say that G-d enjoys the *yerida* itself, as a thing in itself.

When a person reveals that level, he realizes that in a way you can look at it the opposite way: the whole goal of making a *dira b'tachtonim* (a dwelling below), *Moshiach* and all of that, was for us to have the challenge of doing the *avoda*. When a person realizes that the real *kavana* is our *avoda* (as it says, when *Moshiach* comes we are going to yearn for the *avoda* we had in *galus*), even if he does not feel it, as long as he knows it is so, it helps him overcome and be happy right now.

That is one of the things it says in *Tanya*: a *beinoni* should be very happy, even if he never totally overcomes his *yetzer hara*. G-d does not necessarily want you to be a *tzaddik*. It is true that there is a virtue in being a *tzaddik*, but there is also a virtue in the *avoda* itself, in the struggle, and in a way G-d likes that better. So you should be happy that you are doing it. And so we should have the complete *bittul* of the *ra*, where the *etzem hara* gets turned over to good, *v'es ruach hatumah a'avir min ha'aretz*, with the coming of *Moshiach* right away.

reviewQuestions.question: Why does a bribed judge show the difference between the *etzem hamidda* and its *hispashtus*?
Why can a thing be nullified in its opposite only if the opposite is already hidden in it? Give his examples from food and from fire and water.
Why is feeding your hungry enemy, or G-d rewarding the wicked in this world, the strongest *din* of all?
What makes tough love a stronger *chesed* than giving lollipops and presents?
How can *gevura sheb'chesed* and *chesed sheb'gevura* come together, and what does the red pen that writes "green" show about a light in a vessel?
Why can the depth of good and the depth of bad not be included in each other, and how does *mesirus nefesh* turn even the sins of a *baal teshuva* into merits?
